Empirical Research Plan: “Peer Quality, Behavioural Adjustment and Exit‐Exam Performance at Romanian High-Schools”

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Chosen design: Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Design (FRD).

Why RD is appropriate
• Admission to every school × track × cohort cell is governed by a sharp cut-off in the transition score that is known ex-ante and enforced by the Ministry of Education.  
• Students just above and just below a particular cut-off are plausibly identical in all pre-treatment dimensions except that the above-cut-off group is (much) more likely to attend the higher-achieving school/track and to enjoy better peers.  
• Because a small share of students above the cut-off may voluntarily list another school first (and a few below may get in through quota exceptions), treatment is not deterministic ⇒ fuzzy RD, where the cut-off is an instrument for school/peer quality.

All behavioural outcomes (parental effort, homework time, teacher assignment, peer intimidation, etc.) as well as final achievement can be analysed within the same FRD framework by simply changing the dependent variable.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definition
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable
Ti = 1 if student i enrols in the focal higher-achieving school/track in grade 9 (or, more mechanistically, if average peer transition score in her grade is above the town-specific median).

Control group
Students with scores just below the same school-track cut-off who enrol in the next-best school/track inside the same town.

Running variable
Ri = TransitionScorei – Cutoffstc  
(st = school × track, c = cohort).  
Cutoff is known, discrete at 0.

Treatment timing
Event date = first day of 9th grade (September of year c). Outcomes are measured four years later (Baccalaureate) or during high-school (surveys 2005–07).

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes in Ri at 0  
Given the national construction of the transition score and impossibility of partial credit manipulation, potential test scores, parent characteristics, etc. should vary smoothly at the threshold.

A2. No precise manipulation of Ri  
Middle-school teachers have little room to manipulate national exam marks. Density tests (McCrary) are expected to show no discontinuity.

A3. First-stage relevance and monotonicity  
Pr(score ≥ cutoff) causes a discrete jump in probability of attending the focal school/track and in peer quality; nobody reduces the probability of attending the stronger school when their score increases infinitesimally (monotonic).

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA) locally  
The presence of one extra marginal student in a strong school has negligible effect on peers within the small bandwidth.

A5. Homogeneous bandwidth environment  
Within a narrow window (±1.5–2 points) schools do not change curricula, resource allocations, or grading practices discontinuously.

All assumptions are highly plausible in the Romanian setting.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Remedies
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Strategic ranking of schools (selection into treatment)  
• Remedy: FRD already accommodates imperfect compliance; estimate reduced-form and 2SLS LATE.  
• Robustness: restrict sample to students who listed the focal school among their top 3 preferences; results should be similar.

T2. Manipulation of transition scores by middle-school teachers  
• Remedy: Perform McCrary density test; plot covariates vs. Ri.  
• If manipulation is detected in some towns, drop those towns or adopt donut RD (exclude ±0.25 score around 0).

T3. Differential resources (teacher quality, facilities) that change discretely at the cut-off in addition to peers  
• Remedy: Estimate effect of cut-off on measured school inputs (certified teachers, class size).  
• If significant, control for these inputs or conduct a mediation analysis isolating peer-quality channel.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # OLS / IV with clustering
library(rdrobust)     # bias-corrected RD
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
admin   <- fread("romania_admin_2001_2003.csv")   # universe
survey  <- fread("romania_survey_2005_2007.csv")  # 59–64 towns

# 2. Merge & basic variables ----------------------------------------------
setkey(admin, student_id)
setkey(survey, student_id)
dat <- survey[admin]                              # left merge

# Create running variable
dat[, cutoff := cutoff_score]                     # supplied in admin data
dat[, runvar := transition_score - cutoff]

# Treatment indicator: actually attends focal school/track
dat[, treat := as.integer(attend_focal_school == 1)]

# Peer quality (mean transition score within class)
dat[, peer_q := mean(transition_score, na.rm = TRUE),
    by = .(school_id, track, cohort)]

# Outcomes
dat[, bac_z := scale(bac_grade)]                  # standardise for ease
dat[, hw_hours_z := scale(hw_hours_week)]
dat[, parent_volunteer := as.integer(parent_volunteer == "yes")]

# 3. Main FRD specification with rdrobust ---------------------------------
# Bandwidth automatically chosen; cluster by school×track×cohort
frd_bac <- rdrobust(y = dat$bac_z,
                    x = dat$runvar,
                    c = 0,
                    fuzzy = dat$treat,
                    cluster = dat$school_track_cohort)

print(summary(frd_bac))

# 4. Two-stage least squares using fixest (local linear, h = 2) -----------
h <- 2
local <- dat[abs(runvar) <= h]

iv_bac <- feols(bac_z ~ 1 | treat ~ runvar, 
                data = local, 
                cluster = ~school_track_cohort)
summary(iv_bac)

# 5. Robustness check: McCrary density test -------------------------------
mcc <- rddensity(X = dat$runvar, c = 0)
summary(mcc)

# 6. Balance check for baseline covariates --------------------------------
covs <- c("gender", "romani_ethnicity", "parents_college")
for (v in covs){
  bal <- feols(as.formula(paste0(v," ~ runvar + I(runvar>=0)")), 
               data = local, cluster = ~school_track_cohort)
  print(summary(bal))
}

# 7. Behavioural outcome example: homework effort -------------------------
iv_hw <- feols(hw_hours_z ~ 1 | treat ~ runvar, 
               data = local, cluster = ~school_track_cohort)
summary(iv_hw)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Economic theory (peer effects, school quality) predicts positive impacts for marginal students.

Magnitude priors (in SDs):
• Baccalaureate score: +0.20 to +0.30 SD (equivalent to ~0.4–0.6 raw points on a 10-point Romanian scale).  
• Probability of taking the Bacalaureat: +5–8 p.p.  
• Parental inputs (volunteering, tutoring payments): +0.1 SD.  
• Student homework hours: +0.15 SD.  
• Teacher certification share: small to zero once we control for peers (mechanically fixed within school).

Behavioural channels are expected to explain roughly one-half of the achievement gain, with peer quality being the core driver.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Regression Discontinuity)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No sorting/manipulation around the cut-off               = 1  
C2: Baseline covariates smooth at the threshold              = 1  
C3: Large, significant first stage (jump in treatment prob.) = 1  
C4: No other policy/assignment discontinuities at cut-off    = 0.5 (possible school resources jump)  
C5: Results robust to bandwidths / polynomial orders         = 1  

Total = 4.5 / 5 – overall design judged highly credible.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
End of Plan
